q: Are emissions from sending effluent to a common effluent treatment plant (CETP) my Scope 3?
title: Is effluent sent to a CETP my Scope 3?
short: Yes. Effluent you send to a common effluent treatment plant that you do not own or control is Scope 3 Category 5, waste generated in operations, under the GHG Protocol. Your share is the CETP's methane, and its energy use, attributable to the organic load (COD) in your effluent. Your own on-site ETP stays in Scope 1 and 2.
audience: Textile, chemical, pharma and leather units in Indian clusters

sections.h: Where the line between scopes falls
ul: Your own primary treatment or ETP: methane from it is Scope 1, its electricity Scope 2.
The CETP run by a cluster society or SPV that you do not control: its emissions from treating your effluent are your Category 5.
If your unit has an equity stake and you use the equity share approach, include your share of the CETP's Scope 1 and 2 instead, and do not count it twice in Category 5.
Sludge the CETP sends to a secured landfill or co-processing is the CETP's waste, part of the same treatment chain; include it in your Category 5 if the CETP reports it.

p: Many CETPs bill members by volume and pollution load and already measure inlet COD, flow and power use. Ask for the plant's annual electricity, fuel and any biogas captured, plus total inlet COD. Allocate by your share of COD for methane and by your share of volume for pumping energy, then document the key.

sections.h: Fallback: the IPCC method on your discharge
p: Without CETP data, use the IPCC 2006 Volume 5, Chapter 6 method on the COD you discharge: kg COD a year x 0.25 kg CH4 per kg COD x a methane correction factor (MCF) from IPCC Table 6.8 for the CETP's process. Table 6.8 gives 0 for a well managed aerobic plant, 0.3 for an overloaded or poorly managed aerobic plant, 0.8 for an anaerobic reactor or deep lagoon and 0.2 for a shallow lagoon. Measure COD after your own pre-treatment, since that is what the CETP receives.
Carbon dioxide from aerobic treatment is biogenic and is not added. The 2006 IPCC Guidelines treat nitrous oxide from industrial effluent as minor and give no separate method for it.

sections.h: Records an auditor will ask for
ul: CETP membership agreement and monthly charge invoices showing volume.
Your outlet flow meter log and COD test reports.
The CETP's process description, to justify the MCF.
The GWP edition used (IPCC AR5 or AR6) for converting methane to CO2e.

example.title: Worked example: a dyeing unit's CETP share, IPCC fallback
lines: Discharge: 200 kL a day at 1,500 mg COD per litre (1.5 kg per kL) = 300 kg COD a day
Working days: 300; COD a year: 300 x 300 = 90,000 kg
CETP aerobic but overloaded, MCF 0.3: 90,000 x 0.25 x 0.3 = 6,750 kg CH4
CO2e at GWP 28 (IPCC AR5): 6,750 x 28 = 189,000 kg, about 189 t CO2e
If the CETP is a well managed aerobic plant, MCF 0 gives zero methane; only its energy use remains
example.note: The MCF choice moves the result from zero to hundreds of tonnes, so justify it with the CETP's own process description.

senseible: Senseible keeps CETP charge invoices in its separate Scope 3 evidence trail with the source file and SHA-256 fingerprint. The document reader gives no methane figure from a charge invoice alone, since that needs COD and the treatment type; where only the charge is known, a spend-based estimate labelled as such can be provided.
